module: Module 5: Data Subject Rights Level 3 Set

items.lesson_concept: The Right to Erasure or Blocking is not absolute. A PIC can refuse to delete personal data if its retention is required to comply with a legal obligation, such as a court order or tax retention laws[cite: 1].
items.question_text: An executive is under investigation for corporate fraud. Anticipating a subpoena, the executive formally invokes their Right to Erasure, demanding the company's IT department immediately delete their email archives. Can the company lawfully comply with this request?
options: Yes, the Right to Erasure is an absolute constitutional right that overrides corporate policies.
No, because the Right to Erasure cannot be exercised when the personal data is necessary for the establishment, exercise, or defense of legal claims, or to comply with a subpoena.
Yes, but the IT department must keep a metadata log of the deletion.
No, because the executive must pay a deletion fee first.
items.correct_answer: No, because the Right to Erasure cannot be exercised when the personal data is necessary for the establishment, exercise, or defense of legal claims, or to comply with a subpoena.
items.explanation: The Right to Erasure is restricted when data is required for active legal claims, investigations, or statutory retention[cite: 1]. Complying with this request would also likely constitute obstruction of justice.

items.lesson_concept: When a data subject exercises their Right to Object to processing for direct marketing, the PIC must immediately stop processing their data for that specific purpose[cite: 1].
items.question_text: A user clicks 'Opt-Out' to stop receiving targeted advertising from a retail app. The app's automated response states: 'Your objection has been received. Please allow up to 45 business days for our global servers to process this request.' Is this delay legally compliant under the DPA?
options: Yes, 45 days is a globally recognized standard grace period for server synchronization.
No, because when a data subject objects to direct marketing, the PIC is legally obligated to immediately cease processing the data for that purpose without unjustified delay.
Yes, provided they do not sell the data to third parties during those 45 days.
No, the maximum allowable delay is strictly 24 hours.
items.correct_answer: No, because when a data subject objects to direct marketing, the PIC is legally obligated to immediately cease processing the data for that purpose without unjustified delay.
items.explanation: The DPA affords individuals an absolute right to object to direct marketing. The PIC must halt the processing immediately; artificially delaying the opt-out violates this right[cite: 1].

items.lesson_concept: The Right to Access allows data subjects to demand reasonable access to contents of their personal data, sources, recipients, and reasons for disclosure[cite: 1]. It does not extend to intellectual property.
items.question_text: A freelance driver invokes their Right to Access against a ride-hailing company, demanding to see their personal driving history logs AND the proprietary source code of the algorithm the company uses to assign rides. Under the DPA, what must the company disclose?
options: The company must disclose both the driving logs and the algorithm's source code to ensure absolute transparency.
The company is only required to provide the personal driving history logs; the Right to Access does not grant users the right to demand a company's proprietary trade secrets or source code.
The company can deny the entire request because algorithms process data automatically.
The company must provide the algorithm but can withhold the driving logs.
items.correct_answer: The company is only required to provide the personal driving history logs; the Right to Access does not grant users the right to demand a company's proprietary trade secrets or source code.
items.explanation: The Right to Access guarantees an individual the ability to review their own personal data held by the PIC[cite: 1]. It cannot be weaponized to extract corporate intellectual property or trade secrets.

items.lesson_concept: Section 17 explicitly establishes the transmissibility of data subject rights to lawful heirs and assigns after death or incapacity[cite: 1].
items.question_text: Following the sudden death of a public figure, a tabloid publishes unlawfully obtained medical records. The deceased's legally appointed heirs file a complaint with the NPC invoking the Right to Erasure and the Right to Damages. The tabloid argues that privacy rights expire upon death. How will the NPC rule?
options: The NPC will side with the tabloid, as the DPA only protects living natural persons.
The NPC will side with the heirs, as the rights of the data subject are explicitly transmissible to lawful heirs and assigns after death or incapacity.
The NPC will dismiss the case because public figures have no privacy rights.
The NPC will grant the Right to Erasure but deny the Right to Damages.
items.correct_answer: The NPC will side with the heirs, as the rights of the data subject are explicitly transmissible to lawful heirs and assigns after death or incapacity.
items.explanation: Section 17 of the DPA ensures that a data subject's privacy rights do not instantly vanish upon death; they are transmitted to lawful heirs who can invoke them to protect the deceased's data[cite: 1].

items.lesson_concept: The Right to Rectify requires the PIC to correct inaccuracies immediately, unless the request is vexatious or unreasonable[cite: 1].
items.question_text: An internet troll creates a script that submits 5,000 automated 'Right to Rectify' requests per day to a local bank, demanding they change his official title to 'Emperor of the Universe'. Can the bank's Data Protection Officer lawfully ignore these requests?
options: No, the Right to Rectify is absolute and the bank must process every request.
Yes, the PIC can lawfully refuse to act on rectification requests that are manifestly unfounded, unreasonable, or vexatious.
No, but the bank can charge a mandatory administrative fee for each request.
Yes, but only after seeking a formal injunction from the Supreme Court.
items.correct_answer: Yes, the PIC can lawfully refuse to act on rectification requests that are manifestly unfounded, unreasonable, or vexatious.
items.explanation: While the Right to Rectify guarantees the correction of genuine errors, the law protects PICs from having to entertain requests that are clearly vexatious, malicious, or logically impossible[cite: 1].

items.lesson_concept: The Right to Data Portability uniquely ensures that data subjects can obtain their electronically processed data in a structured, commonly used format to move it securely to another system[cite: 1].
items.question_text: A user decides to migrate their business from 'CloudCRM A' to 'CloudCRM B'. They invoke their Right to Data Portability. 'CloudCRM A' provides the data, but completely encrypts it in a highly proprietary format that only 'CloudCRM A' software can read, effectively making it impossible to import into 'CloudCRM B'. Did 'CloudCRM A' comply with the DPA?
options: Yes, because they provided the data and are legally entitled to use proprietary encryption.
No, because Data Portability strictly requires providing the data in an electronic, structured, and commonly used format specifically to allow for further use and prevent vendor lock-in.
Yes, as long as the user did not pay for a premium export feature.
No, because they were required to delete the data instead.
items.correct_answer: No, because Data Portability strictly requires providing the data in an electronic, structured, and commonly used format specifically to allow for further use and prevent vendor lock-in.
items.explanation: The core purpose of Data Portability is interoperability. Providing data in a locked, proprietary format defeats the statutory requirement that the format must allow for 'further use' by the data subject[cite: 1].

items.lesson_concept: The Right to be Informed requires notification before entry into the processing system[cite: 1].
items.question_text: A photo-sharing application updates its Privacy Notice overnight, adding a new clause that allows them to sell all previously uploaded user photos to a facial recognition AI company. They do not notify existing users of this change. Which fundamental data subject right is breached?
options: Right to Data Portability
Right to be Informed, because users must be notified of the specific purpose and scope of processing before it occurs, not retroactively without warning.
Right to Rectify
Right to Damages
items.correct_answer: Right to be Informed, because users must be notified of the specific purpose and scope of processing before it occurs, not retroactively without warning.
items.explanation: The Right to be Informed is violated when a PIC changes the purpose of data processing (especially for existing data) without actively notifying the users and obtaining the necessary consent for the new purpose[cite: 1].

items.lesson_concept: The right to be indemnified applies to damages sustained due to inaccurate, false, unlawfully obtained, or unauthorized use of personal data[cite: 1]. The PIC retains accountability for its PIPs[cite: 1].
items.question_text: A hospital (PIC) hires an external IT firm (PIP) to manage billing. The IT firm negligently exposes the patients' billing records online. A patient suffers severe identity theft and invokes the Right to Damages against the hospital. The hospital claims the patient must sue the IT firm instead. Who is legally accountable to the data subject?
options: Only the IT firm (PIP) is liable since they committed the technical error.
The hospital (PIC) remains fully accountable to the data subject for the breach of data under its control, and the patient can validly seek damages from them.
Neither, because identity theft is a crime committed by third-party hackers.
The National Privacy Commission must pay the damages from a state fund.
items.correct_answer: The hospital (PIC) remains fully accountable to the data subject for the breach of data under its control, and the patient can validly seek damages from them.
items.explanation: Under the principle of accountability, the PIC is ultimately responsible for the data. The data subject exercises their Right to Damages against the PIC, who may then separately seek contractual restitution from their negligent PIP[cite: 1].

items.lesson_concept: A PIC can refuse to delete personal data if its retention is required to comply with a legal obligation[cite: 1].
items.question_text: An individual convicted of money laundering completes their prison sentence. Upon release, they formally demand their bank completely erase their historical transaction records under the 'Right to Erasure/Right to be Forgotten'. The bank refuses, citing a 5-year AMLA record-retention rule. Is the bank's refusal lawful?
options: No, the Right to be Forgotten is an absolute right for rehabilitated citizens.
Yes, the Right to Erasure cannot be exercised when retention is strictly mandated by existing statutory laws, such as AMLA.
No, because the individual has already served their sentence.
Yes, but the bank must immediately surrender the records to the NPC instead.
items.correct_answer: Yes, the Right to Erasure cannot be exercised when retention is strictly mandated by existing statutory laws, such as AMLA.
items.explanation: Data subject rights are not absolute. Statutory legal obligations that mandate data retention take precedence over a subject's request for erasure[cite: 1].

items.lesson_concept: If a subject objects, the PIC must stop processing the data, unless the processing is pursuant to a legal obligation or needed for a legal claim[cite: 1].
items.question_text: A corporate employer uses 'Legitimate Interest' to monitor the web browsing history of its employees on company-owned laptops to prevent malware. An employee exercises their Right to Object, claiming it violates their privacy. What must the employer do to legally continue this processing?
options: They must immediately stop the monitoring without exception.
They must demonstrate that their compelling legitimate interests in network security legally override the employee's objection and privacy rights.
They must force the employee to sign a waiver.
They must transfer the monitoring duties to an external PIP.
items.correct_answer: They must demonstrate that their compelling legitimate interests in network security legally override the employee's objection and privacy rights.
items.explanation: When processing is based on Legitimate Interest and the subject objects, the PIC can only continue if they can prove their compelling legitimate grounds definitively override the fundamental rights of the subject[cite: 1].

items.lesson_concept: The Right to Access allows subjects to demand information on what data is held and the names and addresses of recipients to whom the personal data has been disclosed[cite: 1].
items.question_text: A consumer suspects a loyalty card program is selling their purchasing habits. They file a formal 'Right to Access' request demanding to know exactly which third-party marketing firms received their data. The program refuses, citing 'corporate non-disclosure agreements (NDAs)' with those marketing firms. Which law prevails?
options: The NDAs prevail, as private contracts are protected under civil law.
The Data Privacy Act prevails; the Right to Access guarantees the subject the right to know the identities of the recipients to whom their data was disclosed, overriding the NDAs.
The NDAs prevail, but the program must pay the consumer a royalty fee.
The Data Privacy Act prevails, but only if the consumer pays a legal discovery fee.
items.correct_answer: The Data Privacy Act prevails; the Right to Access guarantees the subject the right to know the identities of the recipients to whom their data was disclosed, overriding the NDAs.
items.explanation: Private corporate NDAs cannot be used to circumvent fundamental statutory rights. The data subject has an absolute right to know who is processing their personal data[cite: 1].

items.lesson_concept: The right to rectify allows a data subject to dispute inaccuracies. The PIC must correct it immediately[cite: 1].
items.question_text: A patient exercises their Right to Rectify to correct a severe misdiagnosis in their central hospital file. The hospital quickly updates their internal database. However, they fail to notify the external health insurance provider they had already sent the erroneous file to, causing the patient's coverage to be unfairly denied. Did the hospital fully comply with the DPA?
options: Yes, the hospital's only obligation is to their internal database.
No, fulfilling the Right to Rectify requires the PIC to ensure that third parties who previously received the erroneous data are informed of the correction.
Yes, the patient is responsible for updating their own insurance.
No, the hospital must pay the patient's medical bills directly.
items.correct_answer: No, fulfilling the Right to Rectify requires the PIC to ensure that third parties who previously received the erroneous data are informed of the correction.
items.explanation: To effectively uphold the Right to Rectify and the principle of Accuracy, the PIC must propagate the correction to external parties to whom the inaccurate data was previously disclosed.

items.lesson_concept: The Right to Erasure applies when the data is incomplete, outdated, false, or unlawfully obtained[cite: 1]. Processing for journalistic purposes is a statutory exemption[cite: 1].
items.question_text: A convicted politician, seeking to rebuild their image, formally demands a national newspaper erase all past digital articles detailing their corruption scandal, citing the 'Right to Erasure'. The newspaper refuses. Under the DPA, who is legally correct?
options: The politician, because the Right to Erasure allows anyone to delete their public history.
The newspaper, because processing personal information exclusively for journalistic purposes is a statutory exemption under the DPA, protecting freedom of the press.
The politician, because corruption records are Sensitive Personal Information requiring consent.
The newspaper, but they must blur the politician's face in the articles.
items.correct_answer: The newspaper, because processing personal information exclusively for journalistic purposes is a statutory exemption under the DPA, protecting freedom of the press.
items.explanation: The Right to Erasure cannot be used to censor legitimate press operations. Section 4 explicitly excludes processing for journalistic purposes to balance privacy with free expression[cite: 1].

items.lesson_concept: The right to file a complaint allows individuals to escalate issues to the NPC[cite: 1]. Generally, subjects should give the PIC an opportunity to address the grievance first.
items.question_text: A user notices a minor typo in their online profile. Without ever contacting the company's support team or Data Protection Officer to request a correction, the user immediately files a formal lawsuit and a complaint with the National Privacy Commission (NPC). How will the NPC likely handle this?
options: The NPC will immediately issue a Cease and Desist Order to the company.
The NPC will likely advise the user to exhaust available internal remedies by first exercising their Right to Rectify directly with the company's DPO.
The NPC will automatically fine the company PHP 1 Million.
The NPC will process the name change themselves.
items.correct_answer: The NPC will likely advise the user to exhaust available internal remedies by first exercising their Right to Rectify directly with the company's DPO.
items.explanation: While the Right to File a Complaint exists[cite: 1], procedural fairness generally requires the data subject to give the PIC an opportunity to address and rectify the issue internally before escalating to a formal regulatory complaint.

items.lesson_concept: Data Portability allows subjects to obtain a copy of their personal data[cite: 1]. This typically covers data provided by the user or generated by their activity, not complex inferred corporate IP.
items.question_text: A user invokes their Right to Data Portability on a credit-scoring app. The app exports all the financial data the user inputted, plus their raw transaction history. However, the app refuses to export the 'Predictive Risk Profile' generated by their proprietary AI. Did the app violate the portability right?
options: Yes, the user owns all data attached to their profile, including AI inferences.
No, the Right to Data Portability generally applies to data provided by the user or generated by their direct activity, not complex, inferred intellectual property created by the PIC.
Yes, but the user must pay for the AI processing costs.
No, because financial apps are exempt from Data Portability.
items.correct_answer: No, the Right to Data Portability generally applies to data provided by the user or generated by their direct activity, not complex, inferred intellectual property created by the PIC.
items.explanation: Portability allows users to move their own structured data to prevent vendor lock-in[cite: 1]. It does not force organizations to hand over derived analytical profiles or proprietary algorithms.

items.lesson_concept: The Right to be Informed requires that the data subject must know the identity of the personal information controller[cite: 1].
items.question_text: A highly targeted political advertisement campaign collects voter data through an interactive quiz website. The website's privacy policy is completely blank regarding who actually owns the site or where the data is sent. Which specific aspect of the Right to be Informed is violated?
options: The right to know the duration of processing.
The right to know the identity and contact details of the Personal Information Controller (PIC).
The right to know the automated decision-making processes.
The right to data portability.
items.correct_answer: The right to know the identity and contact details of the Personal Information Controller (PIC).
items.explanation: A fundamental requirement of the Right to be Informed is transparency regarding the exact identity of the entity (the PIC) that is collecting and holding the personal data[cite: 1].

items.lesson_concept: Lawful heirs and assigns may invoke the data subject's rights after death or incapacity[cite: 1].
items.question_text: A minor suffers a severe cyberbullying incident where an app illegally distributes their private photos. Since the minor lacks legal capacity to file a formal legal complaint, how does the DPA ensure their rights are exercised?
options: The DPA allows the school principal to file the complaint.
Under the principle of transmissibility, the minor's lawful parents or legal guardians can fully invoke the minor's data subject rights on their behalf.
The minor must wait until they turn 18 to file the complaint.
The NPC automatically initiates the case without a complaint.
items.correct_answer: Under the principle of transmissibility, the minor's lawful parents or legal guardians can fully invoke the minor's data subject rights on their behalf.
items.explanation: Transmissibility ensures that when a data subject is legally incapacitated (such as being a minor), their lawful assigns or guardians can step in to exercise their privacy rights[cite: 1].

items.lesson_concept: The right to be indemnified applies for damages sustained due to inaccurate, incomplete, outdated, false, unlawfully obtained, or unauthorized use of personal data[cite: 1].
items.question_text: An automated tenant screening company unlawfully obtains a false criminal record and links it to a citizen's profile. As a result, the citizen is evicted and becomes homeless. Under the DPA, what is the citizen's most powerful legal recourse against the screening company?
options: The Right to Data Portability, to move the false record elsewhere.
The Right to Damages, to be indemnified for the severe harm and damages sustained due to the use of false and unlawfully obtained data.
The Right to be Informed, to ask how the data was obtained.
The Right to Object, to ask them to stop processing.
items.correct_answer: The Right to Damages, to be indemnified for the severe harm and damages sustained due to the use of false and unlawfully obtained data.
items.explanation: When actual harm (like eviction) occurs due to the processing of false or unlawfully obtained data, the Right to Damages empowers the subject to seek financial restitution[cite: 1].

items.lesson_concept: The right to object includes withdrawing consent[cite: 1]. Once withdrawn, processing must stop unless another lawful basis exists.
items.question_text: A user participates in a voluntary medical research study and signs a consent form. Halfway through, the user exercises their Right to Object and withdraws consent. The researchers refuse to delete the user's previously collected data, arguing it will ruin the statistical integrity of the multi-year study. Who is legally correct?
options: The researchers, because scientific data becomes public property.
The user, because withdrawing consent mandates the immediate cessation of processing and the erasure of the data, overriding the study's statistical needs.
The researchers, but they must pay the user a penalty fee.
The user, but they must reimburse the researchers for the disruption.
items.correct_answer: The user, because withdrawing consent mandates the immediate cessation of processing and the erasure of the data, overriding the study's statistical needs.
items.explanation: The Right to Object and withdraw consent is a powerful fundamental right. Unless a specific statutory exemption or legal mandate requires retention, the PIC must respect the withdrawal and cease processing the data[cite: 1].

items.lesson_concept: The right to suspend, withdraw, or order the blocking, removal, or destruction of personal data applies when it is unlawfully obtained or used for unauthorized purposes[cite: 1].
items.question_text: A consumer discovers that a debt collection agency is harassing their employer by using contact information that the agency illegally scraped from a hacked database. Which specific right should the consumer invoke to immediately order the agency to suspend and destroy this contact data?
options: Right to Data Portability
Right to Rectify
Right to Erasure or Blocking, because the data was unlawfully obtained and used for unauthorized purposes.
Right to be Informed
items.correct_answer: Right to Erasure or Blocking, because the data was unlawfully obtained and used for unauthorized purposes.
items.explanation: The Right to Erasure or Blocking is the specific legal mechanism a data subject uses to demand the removal or suspension of data that is being processed unlawfully or for unauthorized harassment[cite: 1].
